title: “I HAVE LEARNED TO BE CONTENT” — THE VERSE THAT COMES BEFORE PHILIPPIANS 4:13
paragraphs: “I HAVE LEARNED TO BE CONTENT” — THE VERSE THAT COMES BEFORE PHILIPPIANS 4:13

Before Paul declared, “I can do all things through Christ,” he confessed something most Christians are still struggling to learn. And once you understand what he really meant, you may never read Philippians 4:13 the same way again.
There is a kind of pain nobody notices because you have become so good at functioning while carrying it.
You still wake up. Still go to work. Still pay what you can. Still answer messages. Still smile when someone asks how you are doing.
You still say, “God is good.”
And you mean it.
But sometimes, when the house grows quiet and nobody is watching, you look at your life and wonder why everything seems to be moving forward for everyone except you.
Someone you grew up with just bought a house.
Someone who started after you is already succeeding.
Someone who once asked you for advice now seems to have everything you have been praying for.
You tap the heart.
You type, “Congratulations! God bless!”
And then you put your phone down.
Not because you hate them.
Not because you are incapable of being happy for someone else.
But because their happiness has somehow reminded you of a prayer you are still waiting for God to answer.
And suddenly, a question rises from somewhere deep inside your exhausted heart.
“Lord, when will it be my turn?”
Maybe you have never said those words aloud.
Maybe you are ashamed that you even think them.
But what if the Scripture you have been quoting for strength is actually inviting you into something far deeper than the breakthrough you have been asking for?
What if Philippians 4:13 was never meant to convince you that you would always get what you wanted?
What if it was written to teach you how to remain faithful to Jesus Christ even when you do not?
Because immediately before Paul wrote one of the most celebrated declarations in Christianity, he wrote something that changes its meaning.
“Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.” — Philippians 4:11, KJV
Read that again.
“I have learned.”
Not “I was born knowing.”
Not “I have never struggled.”
Not “I no longer feel pain.”
Not “Everything finally worked out exactly as I planned.”
I have learned.
And those three words may be the most comforting part of the entire passage.
Because they reveal something about the apostle Paul that many believers desperately need to understand.
Contentment did not come naturally to him.
It was learned.
Through circumstances.
Through dependence.
Through weakness.
Through a life that repeatedly reminded him that Jesus Christ was sufficient even when his surroundings were not.
And perhaps the reason you are struggling so much with contentment is not that you have no faith.
Perhaps you are still learning what Paul had to learn.
But before we go any further, we need to understand what Paul actually said, because a single Greek word opens a window into the heart of this passage.
In Philippians 4:11, the Greek text reads:
ἐγὼ γὰρ ἔμαθον ἐν οἷς εἰμι αὐτάρκης εἶναι
Egō gar emathon en hois eimi autarkēs einai.
A careful translation is:
“For I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am.”
The word translated “content” is αὐτάρκης (autarkēs).
In the Greek world, this word could describe someone who was self-sufficient, someone who possessed enough within himself to remain independent of changing circumstances.
But Paul was not preaching the proud self-reliance of a man who needed nobody.
The surrounding verses make that impossible.
Paul's contentment was rooted in the sufficiency of Christ.
He was not saying, “I am enough.”
He was saying, in effect, “Christ is enough for me to endure what I face.”
That distinction changes everything.
Because the world tells you to become so strong that nothing can hurt you.
Jesus teaches you to depend on Him even when you are weak.
The world tells you that peace comes when you finally control your circumstances.
The Gospel reveals that peace can be found in the Lord even when circumstances remain beyond your control.
And Paul knew the difference.
He did not write Philippians from a comfortable mansion, surrounded by wealth, applauded by crowds, with every earthly desire fulfilled.
He wrote as a prisoner.
Philippians 1:7, 1:13–14, and 1:17 reveal his imprisonment. The traditional understanding places this imprisonment in Rome, although scholars continue to discuss other possible locations.
Wherever the letter was written, one fact is unmistakable.
Paul's freedom was restricted.
His future was uncertain.
His suffering was real.
Yet from that confinement came words that would strengthen believers for centuries.
Think about the irony.
A man whose physical movements were restricted was teaching free people how to live without being imprisoned by their circumstances.
A man facing hardship was teaching others about joy.
A man who had lost so much was declaring that Christ remained his greatest treasure.
And here is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us have unconsciously made a bargain with God.
“Lord, I will be peaceful when You fix my finances.”
“I will be grateful when You heal this relationship.”
“I will be joyful when You open that door.”
“I will stop worrying when I finally know what happens next.”
We do not always say these things directly.
But sometimes our hearts quietly operate as though God's goodness must be proven by the arrival of something we want.
And when it does not arrive, we begin questioning what we once believed.
We still attend church.
We still listen to worship music.
We still share Bible verses.
But somewhere beneath our religious routines, disappointment begins growing roots.
And if we are not careful, those roots can become bitterness.
Not necessarily bitterness toward other people.
Sometimes bitterness toward God.
Because we prayed.
We waited.
We believed.
And the answer did not look the way we expected.
But Paul continues.
“I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.” — Philippians 4:12, KJV
Notice what he includes.
Abundance.
Need.
Fullness.
Hunger.
Paul did not pretend that poverty and plenty were the same experience.
He knew the difference between having enough and going without.
He knew what it meant to receive provision.
He also knew what it meant to experience lack.
And in both conditions, he had learned a secret.
The Greek phrase in verse 12 includes:
μεμύημαι (memyēmai)
It comes from the verb myeō, which can mean to be initiated or instructed into something previously unknown.
Paul was describing a lesson he had come to know through experience.
The secret was not a hidden formula for attracting wealth.
It was not a spiritual technique for avoiding suffering.
It was not a promise that every hardship would disappear if he believed hard enough.
It was the sustaining strength of Christ.
And only after establishing all of that does Paul write:
The Greek reads:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
Literally, the thought is:
“I have strength for all things in the One who strengthens me.”
The immediate context identifies the One who strengthens Paul as Christ.
And the “all things” are not unlimited personal achievements detached from God's will.
They refer to the circumstances Paul has just described.
Having plenty.
Having little.
Being full.
Being hungry.
Experiencing abundance.
Enduring need.
Philippians 4:13 is not a blank check promising that Christians can accomplish every ambition they imagine.
It is a declaration that Christ strengthens His people to remain faithful through the circumstances they are called to face.
That does not make the verse weaker.
It makes it breathtaking.
Because sometimes the greater miracle is not that the prison door opens.
Sometimes the miracle is that your faith survives while the door remains closed.
Sometimes the greater testimony is not that your bank account suddenly overflows.
Sometimes it is that you refuse to surrender your integrity when money is painfully scarce.
Sometimes the victory is not that your grief disappears.
Sometimes it is that you continue trusting Jesus while tears are still falling.
And sometimes the evidence of Christ's strength is not that you feel powerful.
It is that you are still following Him when you know you cannot carry yourself.
But please understand something.
Biblical contentment is not the same as pretending everything is okay.
It is not spiritual numbness.
It is not refusing to grieve.
It is not staying silent about injustice.
It is not remaining in abuse because someone misused Scripture to tell you that a godly person should simply endure.
And it is not an excuse to stop working, planning, seeking help, pursuing healing, or improving your circumstances.
Paul himself sought practical assistance, exercised his legal rights, made plans, worked diligently, and accepted the generous support of fellow believers.
Contentment does not eliminate responsible action.
It changes the condition of your heart while you act.
You can seek a better job without making your job your savior.
You can pray for marriage without believing that singleness makes you incomplete in Christ.
You can work toward financial stability without worshiping money.
You can pursue healing while admitting that you are still hurting.
You can grieve someone you lost while holding on to the hope of the resurrection.
You can tell God that you desperately want your circumstances to change.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39, KJV
That is not a prayer of emotional denial.
That is honest anguish surrendered to the Father's will.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not for feeling pain.
Not for having legitimate needs.
Not for asking God to intervene.
But for allowing our desires to become demands.
For treating God's blessings as more precious than God's presence.
For measuring His love by how quickly He gives us what we ask.
For becoming so focused on the next thing that we stop recognizing His faithfulness in what He has already given.
There is a difference between asking God for something good and believing that life cannot be good unless He gives it to you.
That difference is where contentment begins to grow.
Consider the person who has been praying for financial relief.
Every month feels like a battle.
The bills arrive faster than the income.
They calculate and recalculate.
They give what they can.
They wonder whether one unexpected expense will finally push everything beyond their control.
When they hear someone preach Philippians 4:13 as a guarantee of financial victory, they want to believe it means that the money is coming.
And sometimes God does provide through extraordinary circumstances.
But what happens when the provision comes slowly?
What happens when the answer involves work, sacrifice, help from others, difficult decisions, and long endurance?
Has Christ failed?
No.
Paul's testimony tells us that Christ's sustaining presence is not disproved by seasons of material need.
In fact, the very passage that declares Christ's strength openly acknowledges that believers may experience hunger and lack.
And there is something else we must not overlook.
Paul's contentment did not make the generosity of other Christians unnecessary.
The Philippians had sent support through Epaphroditus.
Paul appreciated their gift.
He recognized their partnership.
He described their generosity as an offering pleasing to God in Philippians 4:18.
This is important.
Paul did not say, “I am content, so nobody should help me.”
And he did not say, “You gave to me, so now God owes you wealth.”
Instead, he rejoiced in their concern, acknowledged their partnership, and directed their attention toward God.
Christian contentment and Christian generosity belong together.
A content heart can receive help without shame.
A generous heart can give without trying to purchase God's favor.
And the church becomes a place where believers bear one another's burdens rather than pretending nobody has any.
Now consider another person.
The one who has been waiting for love.
They have attended weddings.
Smiled for photographs.
Celebrated engagements.
Prayed over relationships that did not last.
And every time somebody says, “Your turn is coming,” they feel the strange mixture of hope and exhaustion that comes from hearing a promise nobody on earth has the authority to guarantee.
What does contentment look like for them?
It does not mean pretending loneliness is imaginary.
It does not mean denying the goodness of marriage.
It means refusing to believe that being unmarried makes them less loved by Christ.
It means remembering that their identity was never supposed to depend on another human being choosing them.
Jesus did not die to make you worthy of love only after someone puts a ring on your finger.
He gave Himself for sinners while they were still sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Before the promotion.
Before the wedding.
Before the restored relationship.
Before the answered prayer.
Before the life you imagined.
Christ loved you.
And that love is not a consolation prize.
It is the foundation of your salvation.
Then there is the believer who feels ashamed of the past.
Maybe you have made decisions that still haunt you.
Maybe your life has chapters you wish nobody knew.
Maybe there was a season when you abandoned convictions you once defended.
Maybe you wounded people.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you walked away from God and then wondered whether you could ever come home.
You see other believers appearing so settled, so disciplined, so spiritually confident.
And you wonder whether contentment is possible for someone carrying your history.
But remember who wrote Philippians.
Paul was once a persecutor of the church.
He had been associated with the violent opposition to followers of Jesus.
He knew what it meant to have a past that could not be undone by human effort.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him, called him, and transformed the direction of his life.
Grace did not make his past righteous.
Grace brought a guilty man to the Savior who justifies the ungodly through faith.
That is the scandal of grace.
God does not declare sin harmless.
He deals with sin through the cross of His Son.
And the same Paul who once persecuted believers later wrote:
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” — Philippians 1:21, KJV
Not “to live is success.”
Not “to live is comfort.”
Not “to live is getting everything I deserve.”
To live is Christ.
This is the center of Philippians.
And this is why the letter cannot be reduced to a collection of motivational slogans.
Its message is anchored in Jesus.
The Jesus who humbled Himself.
The Jesus who took the form of a servant.
The Jesus who became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
The Jesus whom God highly exalted.
Philippians 2:5–11 reveals the pattern of Christ's humility and exaltation.
Before Paul tells believers how to face changing circumstances, he has already pointed them toward the Savior whose obedience led through suffering.
And that matters because Christianity is not built upon the promise that faithful people will never suffer.
It is built upon the crucified and risen Christ.
The cross tells us that suffering is not automatically evidence of God's absence.
The resurrection tells us that suffering and death will not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
And the Gospel tells us that our deepest need is not merely a change in circumstances.
Our deepest need is reconciliation with God.
We have sinned.
We have pursued created things as though they could satisfy what only the Creator can satisfy.
We have sought security, identity, control, and glory apart from Him.
And yet Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and new life by grace.
Not because they finally became content enough to deserve salvation.
Not because they gave enough money.
Not because they performed enough religious activities.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Do you see how liberating that is?
You do not have to turn your life into a perfect success story before you can come to Jesus.
You come because you need Him.
You come with the debt.
With the grief.
With the disappointment.
With the jealousy you are ashamed to admit.
With the ambition that has quietly become an idol.
With the fear that you may never have the life you imagined.
You come honestly.
And you surrender.
Not to a vague idea of positive thinking.
Not to the belief that everything will happen on your preferred schedule.
But to the living Lord Jesus Christ.
And then, little by little, He teaches you a new way to live.
You begin to realize that gratitude is not the denial of hardship.
It is the recognition of God's goodness in the middle of it.
You begin to understand that ambition can be surrendered without being abandoned.
You begin to discover that your neighbor's blessing is not proof that God has forgotten you.
You begin to see that another person's success does not reduce the riches of grace available in Christ.
You begin to pray differently.
Instead of only asking, “Lord, when will You change this?”
You also begin asking, “Lord, how can I honor You here?”
Instead of saying, “I will trust You once I understand,” you learn to say, “Help me trust You even when I do not understand.”
And instead of measuring every day by how much closer you are to your dream, you begin measuring your life by something more enduring.
Are you growing in love?
Are you becoming more truthful?
Are you learning to forgive?
Are you turning away from sin?
Are you caring for others?
Are you becoming more like Jesus?
Because a person can gain everything the world applauds and still have a heart enslaved by endless dissatisfaction.
And a person can possess very little yet enjoy genuine fellowship with God.
That is not romanticizing poverty.
It is recognizing that wealth cannot purchase what only Christ can give.
Paul understood this.
In Philippians 3:8, he declared that he counted all things loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord.
That is the heartbeat behind Philippians 4:13.
Paul's strength was not confidence that he would always rise above every external limitation.
His strength came from the Lord he treasured above every earthly advantage.
And perhaps this explains why the passage feels so different when we read it in context.
The familiar verse says:
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”
But the verses before it tell us what kind of strength Paul was celebrating.
Strength to endure lack without abandoning Christ.
Strength to enjoy abundance without becoming enslaved by it.
Strength to receive generosity with gratitude.
Strength to remain faithful through uncertainty.
Strength to keep living for Jesus when life looks nothing like the picture once held in the heart.
This is not the glamorous strength that always attracts applause.
It is often quiet.
It is the strength of a father who keeps working honestly while worrying about his family's needs.
It is the strength of a mother who prays through tears after everyone else has gone to sleep.
It is the strength of a young believer who refuses to compromise convictions just to be accepted.
It is the strength of a grieving spouse who still whispers the name of Jesus.
It is the strength of someone who has fallen into sin, confesses it, seeks forgiveness, and begins walking in repentance instead of surrendering to despair.
It is the strength of a Christian who can say, “I still wish things were different, but Christ is worthy of my trust today.”
And perhaps one of the most beautiful things about Paul's words is that he never claimed the lesson was automatic.
He learned.
Which means there were experiences through which he came to know it.
And you may be learning too.
You may still struggle with comparison.
You may still feel the sting when another person receives something you deeply desire.
You may still have nights when you cannot understand why God has allowed a particular hardship.
You may still need to confess resentment, envy, fear, or unbelief.
But do not confuse the unfinished work of sanctification with the absence of God's grace.
The Christian life is not the story of people who never struggle.
It is the story of sinners saved by grace, being conformed to the image of Christ.
And sometimes that transformation is painfully slow.
Sometimes it happens through prayers nobody hears.
Sometimes through the humbling experience of receiving help.
Sometimes through relinquishing an expectation that has become an idol.
Sometimes through discovering that what you thought you could not live without was never meant to be your ultimate source of life.
And sometimes through realizing that the greatest gift God has given you is not what is in your hands.
It is the Savior who holds you.
There is a sentence in Hebrews 13:5 that brings this truth into even sharper focus.
“Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” — KJV
Notice the reason given for contentment.
Not “because you will always have enough money.”
Not “because nobody will ever disappoint you.”
Not “because your future will unfold exactly as planned.”
But because God has promised His presence.
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
That does not eliminate the importance of food, shelter, medicine, companionship, and practical support.
Those needs matter.
And Christians should take them seriously.
But the promise reveals the deepest foundation of contentment.
God's faithfulness does not expire when circumstances change.
His people are not abandoned simply because they are suffering.
And for those who belong to Christ, the future ultimately rests not in the strength of their circumstances, but in the faithfulness of their Redeemer.
So perhaps tonight you need to stop asking whether you have achieved enough to be at peace.
Perhaps you need to ask whether you have been expecting a created thing to give you the security that belongs in Christ alone.
The house may still be unfinished.
The savings may still be small.
The relationship may still be unresolved.
The diagnosis may still be frightening.
The opportunity may still be closed.
The grief may still be fresh.
And you may still be waiting.
But you do not have to wait for everything to change before you begin trusting the One who does not change.
You can pray for provision and worship the Provider.
You can pursue healing and cling to the Healer.
You can desire restoration while surrendering the outcome to the Lord.
You can work diligently for tomorrow while receiving today's mercies with thanksgiving.
You can acknowledge your pain without allowing it to become your identity.
And you can say, even through tears:
“Jesus, I still have desires. I still have questions. I still have needs. But I do not want any of those things to become more precious to me than You.”
That is not giving up.
That is surrender.
And surrender to Christ is not defeat.
It is the beginning of freedom from the cruel belief that your life has no value until something else arrives.
If this is exposing something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is bringing to your attention a comparison you have been feeding.
Maybe it is an attitude of entitlement.
Maybe it is a secret resentment.
Maybe it is the exhaustion of trying to earn what God has already offered freely in Christ.
Bring it into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Receive the mercy of the Savior.
And ask Him to teach you what Paul learned.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove your spirituality.
But as a simple prayer from a heart that wants to grow.
Someone reading may need to know that they are not the only believer who has wrestled with these things.
Someone may need to hear how God sustained you, even before your circumstances changed.
And someone may discover that contentment is not an unreachable spiritual achievement reserved for extraordinary Christians.
It is a lesson that ordinary believers can learn through the extraordinary sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
There is also someone in your life who may need this truth.
Perhaps a friend who is silently struggling with comparison.
A family member burdened by financial pressure.
A believer who feels forgotten.
A young person who has mistaken success for identity.
Or someone who has never understood why Christians speak of hope in the middle of suffering.
Because even after we understand the truth, we sometimes need to return to it.

We want this community to be a place where believers are continually brought back to Scripture, where struggling Christians are encouraged to persevere, where those who have wandered are called to repentance, and where people who do not yet know Jesus can encounter the truth of His Gospel.
Not shallow promises.
Not spiritual entertainment dressed up as discipleship.
But the Word of God, the grace of Christ, and the lifelong call to follow Him.
These resources are intended to help people grow deeper in Scripture, understand the Christian faith, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has strengthened your walk with God, there is a meaningful way you can help us continue and expand that work.
Scripture gives us a beautiful picture of believers voluntarily partnering in ministry.
The Philippians supported Paul's work, and he received their generosity with gratitude.
In Philippians 4:17, Paul wrote:
“Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account.”
He valued not merely the material gift, but the spiritual significance of their willing partnership.
That principle matters today.
Supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be an expression of love, generosity, and stewardship.
Your salvation is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be bought.
And your faithfulness to Christ is not measured by whether you can afford to support this particular ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured or compelled.
That is the spirit in which we invite your partnership.
The deeper purpose is the opportunity to participate in work that points people toward Jesus Christ.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can encourage a struggling believer.
Because Gospel ministry is not sustained by money alone.
It is also carried forward through prayer, faithful teaching, generous hearts, honest testimonies, and ordinary Christians willing to speak about the Savior they love.
But before you leave, return with me to that prison.
Imagine Paul again.
Not as a stained-glass figure.
Not as a name printed in the pages of a Bible.
But as a real man.
A man who had experienced opposition.
A man who knew what it meant to suffer.
A man who had received help from believers who loved him.
A man who did not know every detail of what tomorrow would bring.
And yet he wrote:
“I have learned ... to be content.”
He was not celebrating the absence of need.
He was celebrating the sufficiency of Christ.
And then he declared:
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”
Now the words sound different, don't they?
They are no longer merely a slogan to attach to a dream.
They are a confession to carry into hardship.
Christ strengthens me when I have much.
Christ strengthens me when I have little.
Christ strengthens me when I am celebrated.
Christ strengthens me when I am overlooked.
Christ strengthens me when my plans succeed.
Christ strengthens me when obedience leads through suffering.
Christ strengthens me to remain faithful, whatever comes.
And one day, when you look back over your own life, perhaps you will discover that some of the seasons you most wanted to escape became places where you learned to depend upon the Lord more deeply.
Not because every tragedy was good.
Not because every loss was necessary to make you worthy.
Not because pain itself is holy.
But because the God who raised Jesus Christ from the dead is able to sustain His people and work even amid circumstances they would never have chosen.
That is Christian hope.
Not that every earthly desire will be fulfilled.
But that the Savior who gave Himself for us will never cease to be worthy of our trust.
So if you are still waiting, keep praying.
If you are still hurting, bring your grief to Him.
If you have been comparing, confess it.
If you have been wandering, return.
If you have never trusted Christ, turn to Him in repentance and faith.
If you have been measuring your worth by everything you have not yet achieved, remember the cross.
Your deepest need was never merely a better circumstance.
Your deepest need was a Savior.
And Jesus Christ came.
He died.
He rose again.
He saves sinners.
He transforms lives.
He teaches His people to find their deepest treasure in Him.
And that is why the journey from scandal to grace is not merely the story of a ruined reputation becoming respectable.
It is the far greater story of sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The person who once lived for approval can learn to live for Christ.
The person who once worshiped success can learn to worship the Savior.
The person who once believed happiness depended upon having everything can learn the surpassing worth of knowing the One who is Lord over everything.
And the person who has spent years saying, “Lord, I will be content when You finally give me what I want,” can begin to pray something altogether different.
“Lord Jesus, teach me to treasure You above everything I want.”
Because the greatest victory in Philippians 4:13 is not that Paul finally possessed everything he desired.
It is that, in abundance and in need, he had learned to depend upon Christ.
And maybe that is the lesson waiting for us too.
You may still be waiting for your circumstances to change, while Christ is teaching your heart that He is worthy of your trust even before they do.
